120	## Guidance

124	`ReceiptDownloadEndpoint.java:7`. When the response refers to different targets with the same filename, include the
125	smallest subset of each target's full path that lets the reader distinguish them; otherwise do not include a directory
126	in the description. The target may use the full available path. Before finalizing, reject a bracketed local-file label
127	such as `[ReceiptDownloadEndpoint.java:7]` unless it has the Markdown link target required by this rule; brackets alone
128	are not a link. Write the target immediately after `(` and before `)`, without leading or trailing whitespace.

131	# Intermediate versus Terminal Goals
132	
133	## Guidance
134	
135	For every workflow, name the terminal goal and the acceptance evidence that proves it. Classify plans, staging
136	artifacts, repairs, migrations, investigations, commits, recorded transitions, and verification as intermediate tasks
137	unless their evidence proves every terminal acceptance condition.
138	
139	Record every required terminal gate and its required evidence before execution. Mark each gate passed, failed, unrun, or
140	explicitly excluded by the user; do not infer a passed state from a related check. A failed or unrun required gate is an
141	unmet terminal condition. A clean build, an inspected result, a repaired intermediate artifact, or an existing sequence
142	of commits cannot substitute for the gate that the workflow requires.
143	
144	Match evidence to the claim each terminal gate makes. Evidence that establishes only an enabling condition—such as
145	installation, configuration, authorization, discovery, connection, initialization, or process start—may pass only an
146	availability gate. It cannot pass a behavior or outcome gate. For those gates, require evidence from the relevant
147	execution boundary that the required behavior ran and produced its required effect. When availability itself is the
148	terminal outcome, record availability as that gate's claim.
149	
150	When new work arises, classify it before acting. It supports the current terminal goal unless the user explicitly
151	replaces or expands that goal. Record its own completion evidence separately. After it completes, re-evaluate the
152	unchanged terminal conditions and continue from the next unmet condition. Do not report completion, return control as
153	complete, or discard required follow-up work on intermediate evidence.
154	
155	Treat a user instruction as a goal change only when it explicitly replaces or expands the requested terminal outcome. A
156	discovered prerequisite, failure, repair, workaround, or implementation detail does not change that outcome merely
157	because completing it is necessary to proceed.
158	
159	Before an irreversible action that represents completion—such as committing, finalizing, publishing, or declaring a
160	workflow complete—record the user-authorized scope and compare it with terminal acceptance evidence. Every scoped item
161	must have completion evidence or an explicit user-authorized exclusion. A prior result may reduce the remaining scope
162	only when durable evidence proves it covered the same item under the same governing contract; a tidy-looking history, an
163	earlier status claim, or partial inspection is intermediate evidence, not proof. Otherwise continue across the full
164	authorized scope. Immediately before the terminal action or claim, repeat that comparison, including the recorded gate
165	states, and report remaining work instead of success when any item is unaccounted for or any required gate is failed or
166	unrun.

169	# Target Audience
170	
171	## Guidance
172	
173	Write every user response, prompt or rule file, source comment or Javadoc, command help text, and error message so its
174	intended reader can identify the relevant actor, input or state, action, result, and next decision without knowing this
175	project's vocabulary.
176	
177	Prefer common precise language. Introduce a specialized or abstract workflow term only when it conveys a distinction
178	that common language loses; define it at its first reader-visible use in concrete terms. Do not define a term by
179	repeating it or replacing it with other undefined project terms. When a plain definition still needs workflow
180	vocabulary, add the shortest before-to-after example that shows the ordinary observable effect. For example, replace
181	“whole later correction commit” with “a later commit containing only changes that complete or correct one earlier
182	feature.”
183	
184	Apply the same test to a new category, exception, boundary, or conclusion. It is unexplained when a reader must accept a
185	label such as “family”, “complete”, or “required” without being told which observable facts make it true and what
186	decision those facts require. Do not let an example or desired result define that boundary. At its first use, name the
187	actor, observable facts, acceptance evidence, and resulting decision; then check one meaningful analogous case and one
188	dissimilar case to ensure the wording states the shared condition rather than the example's label.
189	
190	Do not use an internal state or compound relationship label as its own explanation in reader-facing prose. Name the
191	artifact or action it represents and why it matters. When the label conceals why an operation cannot work in a receiving
192	state, explain the smallest causal sequence before proposing a remedy: the original and receiving states, operation,
193	assumption missing from the receiving state, and observable result. Then create a version of the selected operation that
194	relies only on the receiving state and verify its intended result. When the workflow lacks that capability, say that the
195	workflow and tool need a feature to create and verify it; do not imply that the change is impossible.
196	
197	When warning that a check, observation, or result cannot establish a conclusion, explain the failed reasoning as an
198	observable sequence. Name the check or observation, the conclusion it might lead the reader to draw, the inputs or cases
199	it leaves unexamined, and the resulting incorrect decision. Then state the replacement procedure: which artifacts or
200	inputs to examine, the comparison or decision to make, and the evidence that completes it. Do not say only that the
201	reader must not rely on, assume, or treat something as proof; that does not explain why it is insufficient or how to
202	obtain the missing evidence.
203	
204	When explaining a diagnosis, do not replace observed evidence and its limited conclusion with an internal label such as
205	"the model-facing boundary." First name the producer, the artifact, the differing observed values, and the resulting
206	behavior in their causal order. Then state only what those observations establish. If the unobserved step that changes a
207	value is not yet known, say that it remains to be located and name the next check; do not assign it to a component merely
208	because it lies between two observations.
209	
210	For example, a patch prepared after `addsValidation()` exists can rely on that unchanged nearby text. When an earlier
211	commit lacks the method, Git cannot locate the patch. Create a version relative to that earlier commit and verify it. Do
212	not lead with labels such as “source tree,” “destination tree,” “target-adapted,” “reconstruction,” or “context” unless
213	the reader has first been given this explanation or the term is immediately defined in it.
214	
215	Do not explain ordinary, broadly understood technical terms unless the project gives them a specialized meaning.
216	
217	Before finalizing prose, review the actual draft—not only these guidelines—for internal labels, compound relationship
218	labels, and unexplained workflow terms. For each one, either replace it with the concrete artifact, relationship, and
219	action it hides, or define it where it first appears. Then ask whether the intended reader can paraphrase the sentence,
220	identify the required action or decision, and explain any necessary specialized term without reading another artifact.
221	Rewrite it when the answer is no.
222	
223	---
224	# User Request Scheduling
225	
226	## Guidance
227	
228	When a user request arrives during active work, acknowledge receiving it immediately. Classify it using the Intermediate
229	versus Terminal Goals rule.
230	
231	When the request relates to the current terminal goal, treat it as steering for the current work and apply it
232	immediately. An explicit request to stop, cancel, replace, or do work instead of the current goal is related steering
233	that changes the terminal goal; apply it immediately and retain or discard queued goals only as the user directs. When
234	the request is unrelated, append it to the queued goals after every request already queued; process queued goals
235	first-come-first-served after the current terminal goal completes.
236	
237	When translating a user request into a tool or workflow invocation, supply an optional limit, policy, or setting only
238	when the user explicitly provides it or the request identifies the project's documented default. Authorization to use a
239	capability does not authorize selecting its optional parameters. For example, create or resume a goal without a token
240	budget unless the user states one; pass a stated budget exactly.

# File Links

## Guidance

When a reader-visible response refers to a local file, use a Markdown link: `[Description](target)`. The description
must contain the target's filename and, when available, append a colon followed by its decimal line number, such as
`ReceiptDownloadEndpoint.java:7`. When the response refers to different targets with the same filename, include the
smallest subset of each target's full path that lets the reader distinguish them; otherwise do not include a directory
in the description. The target may use the full available path. Before finalizing, reject a bracketed local-file label
such as `[ReceiptDownloadEndpoint.java:7]` unless it has the Markdown link target required by this rule; brackets alone
are not a link. Write the target immediately after `(` and before `)`, without leading or trailing whitespace.

---
# Intermediate versus Terminal Goals

## Guidance

For every workflow, name the terminal goal and the acceptance evidence that proves it. Classify plans, staging
artifacts, repairs, migrations, investigations, commits, recorded transitions, and verification as intermediate tasks
unless their evidence proves every terminal acceptance condition.

Record every required terminal gate and its required evidence before execution. Mark each gate passed, failed, unrun, or
explicitly excluded by the user; do not infer a passed state from a related check. A failed or unrun required gate is an
unmet terminal condition. A clean build, an inspected result, a repaired intermediate artifact, or an existing sequence
of commits cannot substitute for the gate that the workflow requires.

Match evidence to the claim each terminal gate makes. Evidence that establishes only an enabling condition—such as
installation, configuration, authorization, discovery, connection, initialization, or process start—may pass only an
availability gate. It cannot pass a behavior or outcome gate. For those gates, require evidence from the relevant
execution boundary that the required behavior ran and produced its required effect. When availability itself is the
terminal outcome, record availability as that gate's claim.

When new work arises, classify it before acting. It supports the current terminal goal unless the user explicitly
replaces or expands that goal. Record its own completion evidence separately. After it completes, re-evaluate the
unchanged terminal conditions and continue from the next unmet condition. Do not report completion, return control as
complete, or discard required follow-up work on intermediate evidence.

Treat a user instruction as a goal change only when it explicitly replaces or expands the requested terminal outcome. A
discovered prerequisite, failure, repair, workaround, or implementation detail does not change that outcome merely
because completing it is necessary to proceed.

Before an irreversible action that represents completion—such as committing, finalizing, publishing, or declaring a
workflow complete—record the user-authorized scope and compare it with terminal acceptance evidence. Every scoped item
must have completion evidence or an explicit user-authorized exclusion. A prior result may reduce the remaining scope
only when durable evidence proves it covered the same item under the same governing contract; a tidy-looking history, an
earlier status claim, or partial inspection is intermediate evidence, not proof. Otherwise continue across the full
authorized scope. Immediately before the terminal action or claim, repeat that comparison, including the recorded gate
states, and report remaining work instead of success when any item is unaccounted for or any required gate is failed or
unrun.

---
# Target Audience

## Guidance

Write every user response, prompt or rule file, source comment or Javadoc, command help text, and error message so its
intended reader can identify the relevant actor, input or state, action, result, and next decision without knowing this
project's vocabulary.

Prefer common precise language. Introduce a specialized or abstract workflow term only when it conveys a distinction
that common language loses; define it at its first reader-visible use in concrete terms. Do not define a term by
repeating it or replacing it with other undefined project terms. When a plain definition still needs workflow
vocabulary, add the shortest before-to-after example that shows the ordinary observable effect. For example, replace
“whole later correction commit” with “a later commit containing only changes that complete or correct one earlier
feature.”

Apply the same test to a new category, exception, boundary, or conclusion. It is unexplained when a reader must accept a
label such as “family”, “complete”, or “required” without being told which observable facts make it true and what
decision those facts require. Do not let an example or desired result define that boundary. At its first use, name the
actor, observable facts, acceptance evidence, and resulting decision; then check one meaningful analogous case and one
dissimilar case to ensure the wording states the shared condition rather than the example's label.

Do not use an internal state or compound relationship label as its own explanation in reader-facing prose. Name the
artifact or action it represents and why it matters. When the label conceals why an operation cannot work in a receiving
state, explain the smallest causal sequence before proposing a remedy: the original and receiving states, operation,
assumption missing from the receiving state, and observable result. Then create a version of the selected operation that
relies only on the receiving state and verify its intended result. When the workflow lacks that capability, say that the
workflow and tool need a feature to create and verify it; do not imply that the change is impossible.

When warning that a check, observation, or result cannot establish a conclusion, explain the failed reasoning as an
observable sequence. Name the check or observation, the conclusion it might lead the reader to draw, the inputs or cases
it leaves unexamined, and the resulting incorrect decision. Then state the replacement procedure: which artifacts or
inputs to examine, the comparison or decision to make, and the evidence that completes it. Do not say only that the
reader must not rely on, assume, or treat something as proof; that does not explain why it is insufficient or how to
obtain the missing evidence.

When explaining a diagnosis, do not replace observed evidence and its limited conclusion with an internal label such as
"the model-facing boundary." First name the producer, the artifact, the differing observed values, and the resulting
behavior in their causal order. Then state only what those observations establish. If the unobserved step that changes a
value is not yet known, say that it remains to be located and name the next check; do not assign it to a component merely
because it lies between two observations.

For example, a patch prepared after `addsValidation()` exists can rely on that unchanged nearby text. When an earlier
commit lacks the method, Git cannot locate the patch. Create a version relative to that earlier commit and verify it. Do
not lead with labels such as “source tree,” “destination tree,” “target-adapted,” “reconstruction,” or “context” unless
the reader has first been given this explanation or the term is immediately defined in it.

Do not explain ordinary, broadly understood technical terms unless the project gives them a specialized meaning.

Before finalizing prose, review the actual draft—not only these guidelines—for internal labels, compound relationship
labels, and unexplained workflow terms. For each one, either replace it with the concrete artifact, relationship, and
action it hides, or define it where it first appears. Then ask whether the intended reader can paraphrase the sentence,
identify the required action or decision, and explain any necessary specialized term without reading another artifact.
Rewrite it when the answer is no.

---
# User Request Scheduling

## Guidance

When a user request arrives during active work, acknowledge receiving it immediately. Classify it using the Intermediate
versus Terminal Goals rule.

When the request relates to the current terminal goal, treat it as steering for the current work and apply it
immediately. An explicit request to stop, cancel, replace, or do work instead of the current goal is related steering
that changes the terminal goal; apply it immediately and retain or discard queued goals only as the user directs. When
the request is unrelated, append it to the queued goals after every request already queued; process queued goals
first-come-first-served after the current terminal goal completes.

When translating a user request into a tool or workflow invocation, supply an optional limit, policy, or setting only
when the user explicitly provides it or the request identifies the project's documented default. Authorization to use a
capability does not authorize selecting its optional parameters. For example, create or resume a goal without a token
budget unless the user states one; pass a stated budget exactly.

# Actionable Documentation Coverage

## Design Goals

- Ensure an artifact-wide documentation audit verifies that each document enables its reader to make the required
  decisions, not merely that documentation is present or syntactically valid, and excludes facts that do not support
  those decisions.

## Guidance

When applying documentation conventions across existing code or documentation, inventory every in-scope document
section, code comment, type, function, method, script, command, and configuration entry. For each, record its intended
reader and the decision that reader must make. Then check that the wording gives the reader the information needed to
act: concrete responsibility or behavior, applicable inputs and outputs, caller-visible state changes and failures,
and—when the name does not make it clear—when to use it or what to do next.

Classify whether the information required for each reader decision is directly stated, safely implied by a plainly named
operation, or missing. Do not accept an internal label, implementation mechanism, or compressed project term as a
description of behavior or a use condition. Check every caller-visible side effect, including a supplied resource that
the operation closes, replaces, or consumes. Rewrite every missing or misleading description, then recheck the complete
inventory rather than only the reported example.

For every retained fact, identify the reader decision, action, right, obligation, or verification it supports. Remove
provenance, generation or rendering mechanics, prior presentation, editing history, and other implementation details
when they support none. Retain a mechanism only when the reader must use it or know it to predict behavior, exercise a
right or obligation, recover from failure, or verify the documented claim.
